\section[va]{\ml{വ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S110-letter-va}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ഇ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{വ}}
\textbf{\ml{വ}} — \emph{va}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{v}, it is \textbf{va}.

This chapter's farewells are built on a verb that starts with it, and the verb itself arrives on the next page.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{വരിക}} \emph{varika} — to come
\end{itemize}

Every farewell this chapter is heading for is built on it, so the shape is worth having in hand first.

\section[u]{\ml{ഉ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S116-letter-u}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{വ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{ഉ}}
\textbf{\ml{ഉ}} — \emph{u}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel} — the shape this vowel takes when a word \emph{begins} with it, rather than the sign it becomes inside a word.

Every Malayalam verb you are about to meet ends in the same two letters, \textbf{\ml{ഉക}} \emph{-uka}, and this is the first of them.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{ഉക}} \emph{-uka} — the ending that makes a Malayalam verb's dictionary form
\end{itemize}

You already read its sign form, \textbf{\ml{◌ു}}, in the name \textbf{\ml{അരുൺ}}. Where the vowel opens a syllable instead of riding on a consonant, it needs the full letter \textbf{\ml{ഉ}}.

\section[pōkuka]{\ml{പോകുക} (pōkuka) — \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} and \ml{വരിക} (to come)}

\label{lesson:ML-C04-pokuka}



\begin{quote}
Two everyday verbs — and together they make the Malayalam goodbye.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{പോ}} (\emph{pō}, \emph{pa} + long-\emph{ō} sign) + \textbf{\ml{കുക}} (\emph{kuka}, the dictionary \textquotedblleft{}-uka\textquotedblright{} ending) $\to$ \textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} (\emph{pōkuka}). Its partner: \textbf{\ml{വരിക}} (\emph{varika}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}).

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} (\emph{pōkuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}) and \textbf{\ml{വരിക}} (\emph{varika}, \textquotedblleft{}to come\textquotedblright{}) are native Dravidian verbs. Notice the ending \textbf{-\ml{ഉക}} (\emph{-uka}) — this is how Malayalam names a verb in the dictionary, its \textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} form (where Tamil uses a bare stem). Malayalam, like all its family, does not say a plain \textquotedblleft{}goodbye\textquotedblright{}: it says \textquotedblleft{}I go, and I \textbf{come back}.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}pōkuka\textquotedblright{} (to go) and \textquotedblleft{}varika\textquotedblright{} (to come)
  \item the \textquotedblleft{}to \_\_\_\textquotedblright{} ending every Malayalam verb takes (\emph{-uka})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending marks a Malayalam infinitive, and why do you need both \textquotedblleft{}go\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}come\textquotedblright{} to say goodbye? (\emph{-uka}; the farewell is \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ū]{\ml{◌ൂ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:ML-S141-vowel-sign-uu}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \ml{ഉ} — what does it do?

One character this time. One only. It has not been on a page yet: it arrives with the word on the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \ml{◌ൂ}}
\textbf{\ml{◌ൂ}} — \emph{ū}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign}. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and \textbf{replaces} the \emph{a} built into it with \emph{ū}. Replaces, not adds — the \emph{a} is gone.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\ml{വരൂ}} \emph{varū} — \textquotedblleft{}come!\textquotedblright{}, the short command you meet on the next page
\end{itemize}

It is the long partner of \textbf{\ml{◌ു}}, the sign you read in \textbf{\ml{അരുൺ}}. Same place under the consonant, same vowel, held longer — and the shape grows a second loop to say so.

Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

\section[pōyi varāṁ]{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരാം} (pōyi varāṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C04-poyi-varaam}



\begin{quote}
The everyday Malayalam goodbye — a promise, not a parting.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{പോയി}} (\emph{pōyi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{pō} + the \textquotedblleft{}-yi\textquotedblright{} that means \textquotedblleft{}having …d.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{\ml{വരാം}} (\emph{varāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}{[}I{]} will come\textquotedblright{}) is \emph{va} + the \textbf{-\ml{ആം}} (\emph{-āṁ}) ending, \textquotedblleft{}I/we will / let me.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരാം}} = \textbf{\ml{പോയി}} (\emph{pōyi}, \textquotedblleft{}having gone\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{വരാം}} (\emph{varāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}I'll come\textquotedblright{}) — literally \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{having gone, I'll come {[}back{]}},\textquotedblright{} i.e. \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{} A Malayali never signs off with a bare \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving.\textquotedblright{} It is the same \textquotedblleft{}go-and-come-back\textquotedblright{} farewell across the Dravidian south (Tamil \emph{pōy varugiṟēṉ}, Kannada \emph{hōgi baruttēne}, Telugu \emph{veḷḷi vastānu}). The warm reply is \textbf{\ml{പോയി} \ml{വരൂ}} (\emph{pōyi varū}, \textquotedblleft{}go and come {[}back{]}\textquotedblright{}).

It reaches past Dravidian, too: Bengali, an Indo-Aryan language with no shared ancestor for these words, says goodbye with \emph{āshi} — \textquotedblleft{}I come.\textquotedblright{} The whole south, and beyond, prefers a promise of return to a blunt farewell.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -\ml{ആം} ending, \textquotedblleft{}let me / I will\textquotedblright{}}]
\textbf{-\ml{ആം}} (\emph{-āṁ}) added to a verb stem means \textquotedblleft{}I/we will\textquotedblright{} or \textquotedblleft{}let me\textquotedblright{} — a soft, volitional future: \emph{varāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll come\textquotedblright{}), \emph{kāṇāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}let's see,\textquotedblright{} coming next lesson), \emph{ceyyāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll do it\textquotedblright{}). It is Malayalam's gentle way of promising an action.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the goodbye — \emph{pōyi varāṁ}
  \item its literal meaning (\textquotedblleft{}having gone, I'll come\textquotedblright{} $\to$ \textquotedblleft{}I'll come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{pōyi varū}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the Malayalam goodbye literally promise, and what does the \emph{-āṁ} ending add? (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{}; \emph{-āṁ} = \textquotedblleft{}I will / let me.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nāḷe kāṇāṁ]{\ml{നാളെ} \ml{കാണാം} (nāḷe kāṇāṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C04-naale-kaanaam}



\begin{quote}
A goodbye with a date on it — and the \emph{-āṁ} ending you just met.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} (\emph{nāḷe}): \textbf{\ml{നാ}} (\emph{nā}) + \textbf{\ml{ളെ}} (\emph{ḷe}, with the retroflex \textbf{\ml{ള}} \emph{ḷ}). \textbf{\ml{കാണാം}} (\emph{kāṇāṁ}) = \emph{kāṇ} (\textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{}) + the \textbf{-\ml{ആം}} (\emph{-āṁ}) ending, \textquotedblleft{}let's.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} (\emph{nāḷe}, \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}) is native Dravidian, from \textbf{\ml{നാൾ}} (\emph{nāḷ}, \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{}) — the very same \emph{nāḷ} behind Tamil's \emph{nāḷai} and Kannada's \emph{nāḷe}. \textbf{\ml{കാണാം}} (\emph{kāṇāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}let's see\textquotedblright{}) is from \textbf{\ml{കാണുക}} (\emph{kāṇuka}, \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}) + \emph{-āṁ} — so the phrase is \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow, let's see {[}each other{]}}.\textquotedblright{} One family, one word for \textquotedblleft{}day,\textquotedblright{} one habit of parting until the next.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}nāḷe kāṇāṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word for \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ}, shared with Tamil \& Kannada)
  \item the verb \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kāṇ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two pieces of \emph{nāḷe kāṇāṁ}, and what Dravidian sisters share the \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} root? (\emph{Nāḷe} \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} + \emph{kāṇ} \textquotedblleft{}see\textquotedblright{}; Tamil \emph{nāḷai}, Kannada \emph{nāḷe} — all from \emph{nāḷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[vīṇḍuṁ kāṇāṁ]{\ml{വീണ്ടും} \ml{കാണാം} (vīṇḍuṁ kāṇāṁ) — \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ML-C04-veendum-kaanaam}



\begin{quote}
The open-ended, warm goodbye — no date, just a promise.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The letters in this word}
\textbf{\ml{വീണ്ടും}} (\emph{vīṇḍuṁ}): note the retroflex cluster \textbf{\ml{ണ്ട}} (\emph{ṇḍ}) and the final \emph{anusvāra}. \textbf{\ml{കാണാം}} (\emph{kāṇāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}let's see\textquotedblright{}) you just learned.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ml{വീണ്ടും} \ml{കാണാം}} = \textbf{\ml{വീണ്ടും}} (\emph{vīṇḍuṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{}) + \textbf{\ml{കാണാം}} (\emph{kāṇāṁ}, \textquotedblleft{}let's see\textquotedblright{}) — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{we'll see {[}each other{]} again}.\textquotedblright{} Both words are native Dravidian: \emph{vīṇḍuṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}again,\textquotedblright{} from \emph{vīṇṭu}, \textquotedblleft{}to return\textquotedblright{}) and \emph{kāṇ} (\textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}). Where Tamil's \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} reaches for the Sanskrit loan \emph{sandi} to say \textquotedblleft{}meet,\textquotedblright{} Malayalam — like Kannada — keeps its own native verb, here \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}vīṇḍuṁ kāṇāṁ\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}let's see\textquotedblright{} (\emph{vīṇḍuṁ}, \emph{kāṇāṁ})
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does the phrase mean, and which native verb does Malayalam use instead of Tamil's Sanskrit \emph{sandi}? (\textquotedblleft{}We'll see {[}each other{]} again\textquotedblright{}; \emph{kāṇ}, \textquotedblleft{}to see.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Chapter 4 — The farewells}

\label{lesson:ML-C04-practice}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Three ways to part — none of them a blunt \textquotedblleft{}goodbye.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange — the farewells}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the everyday goodbye — \emph{pōyi varāṁ} (\textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item the warm reply — \emph{pōyi varū} (\textquotedblleft{}go and come back\textquotedblright{})
  \item \textquotedblleft{}see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{} — \emph{nāḷe kāṇāṁ}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}we'll meet again\textquotedblright{} — \emph{vīṇḍuṁ kāṇāṁ}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn — the atoms}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two verbs and their \textquotedblleft{}-uka\textquotedblright{} form (\emph{pōkuka} go, \emph{varika} come)
  \item \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} inside \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} (\emph{nāḷ}), \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} (\emph{vīṇḍuṁ}), \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{} (\emph{kāṇ})
  \item the \emph{-āṁ} ending — \textquotedblleft{}I will / let's\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{pōyi varāṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}having gone, I'll come\textquotedblright{}; the Dravidian promise-of-return goodbye
  \item \emph{nāḷe} $\leftarrow$ \emph{nāḷ} \textquotedblleft{}day\textquotedblright{} (shared with Tamil \& Kannada); \emph{kāṇ} \textquotedblleft{}to see\textquotedblright{}
  \item \emph{vīṇḍuṁ} \textquotedblleft{}again\textquotedblright{} — where Tamil borrowed Sanskrit \emph{sandi}, Malayalam kept \emph{kāṇ}
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

  \item \textbf{\ml{പോകുക}} — \textbf{\ml{ഉ}} \emph{u}, the vowel inside the ending \textbf{\ml{ഉക}}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does Malayalam never say a plain \textquotedblleft{}I'm leaving,\textquotedblright{} and what does its everyday goodbye promise instead? (It sounds too final; \emph{pōyi varāṁ} promises \textquotedblleft{}I'll go and come back.\textquotedblright{})
\end{tcolorbox}
